assignments.name: Mock interviews and reflections
assignments.description: Students rotate through interviewer, candidate, and observer in three rounds: a coding interview, a data task built on the Cookie Cats mobile game A/B test, and a consulting-style case (Heartcorp, pricing a new cardiac stent). The interviewer scores the candidate against a rubric, and everyone writes a one to two page reflection on what the other side of the table taught them.

assignments.name: Onboarding plan
assignments.description: A two to three page 30/60/90-day onboarding guide for a new technical hire, built around a small first win, or a critique and redesign of a real company's public onboarding program such as GitLab's.

assignments.name: Group case analyses
assignments.description: Cases worked in teams during the in-person week in Doha. In the Doha Foundation case, a funding board has $120 million and twenty reviewed proposals; each group uses an assigned decision method, from the rational model to dialectical inquiry to Delphi, and reports what it learned about deciding across cultures. In Managing a Global Team, a 45-person support team at Sun Microsystems spread across four countries misses an outage; teams diagnose the root causes and present a 30-day plan. Project Phoenix is a mobile banking app at month four of six, with 70% of the budget spent and 40% of the features done.

assignments.name: Management reflection
assignments.description: A short paper on the strategy and tactics each student will use when they manage technical people.

projects.term: Group case: Managing a Global Team at Sun Microsystems, Fall 2025

items.subject: Team 1
items.approach: Root causes, a 30-day plan, and one long-term change
items.description: One team traced the outage to unclear cross-site ownership, cultural misreadings and leadership communication. It recommended a single global escalation protocol, rebuilding the support queue with cross-site validation, a leads-only international meeting, site-by-site trust conversations and letting sites act without waiting for the U.S., with a global team charter of shared norms as the long-term change.

items.subject: Team 2
items.approach: Root causes, a 30-day plan, and one long-term change
items.description: A second team blamed the absence of global process ownership, over-reliance on the U.S. team and cultural friction. It proposed manager-level cross-site reviews, sharing decisions with all sites at once, one emergency rule, a single owner for customer data and a rotating time-zone meeting schedule (U.S.-, Asia- and Euro-Asia-priority slots), plus an annual rotating in-person retreat and a unified Global Operations Playbook.

items.subject: Team 3
items.approach: Root causes, a 30-day plan, and one long-term change
items.description: A third team stressed low trust, perceived inequity in task allocation and pay, and weak cultural awareness. It recommended a weekly global sync at rotating times with local pre-meetings, giving high-visibility work to the India and UAE sites, documenting decisions within 24 hours, a clear outage process and regional listening sessions with 1:1s, plus a company-wide 'Global Operating System' as the long-term change.
